text:
Coordinated campus programs, faculty incentives and startup courses power Berkeley's entrepreneurial surge Connecting scattered campus programs and overhauling top-down incentives turned the University of California (UC), Berkeley, into the world’s leading producer of startup founders, a university official said Tuesday, offering a blueprint for other institutions.
“Turns out it’s not rocket science,” Darren Cooke, the university’s chief innovation and entrepreneurship officer, said in a keynote speech at the Times Higher Education (THE) Innovation & Impact Summit 2026 in Seoul.
UC Berkeley, a public university in California’s San Francisco Bay area, edged out nearby Stanford University four years ago in PitchBook’s annual ranking of universities whose alumni found venture-backed startups and has widened its lead since, Cooke said. PitchBook is a U.S. data firm that tracks venture capital deals.
The first step, he said, is getting people together. About 70 campus organizations sit on a single council that meets monthly. Each must report at least one “win” a month and can ask the others for help.
“This is the magic, actually,” Cooke said, noting that the other nine University of California campuses do not run such a council.
UC Berkeley launched the Bakar Fellows Program in 2012 to give faculty translational research grants aimed at commercialization. Cooke said 84 faculty members have received grants of about $300,000, producing 40 companies, though starting one is not required.
The 10-campus UC system has also told its chancellors that patenting, licensing and startup creation count as a plus in tenure reviews, the evaluations that decide whether professors receive permanent appointments, Cooke said.
Faculty incentives also came up earlier at the summit, where Park Jhung-soo, executive vice president for research and external affairs at Ewha Womans University, said Korean professors are still evaluated mainly by their papers.
Cooke also highlighted Berkeley Changemaker, a program launched in 2020 that brings entrepreneurial thinking into about 50 courses across subjects. More than 13,000 students have taken at least one class. Founding a startup “requires kind of a unique DNA,” he said, but all students benefit from thinking like an entrepreneur.
The focus extends to the top. Rich Lyons, a former dean of Berkeley’s Haas School of Business, became the campus’ first chief innovation and entrepreneurship officer in 2020 and has served as chancellor since July 2024.
Cooke described a student who, after her grandfather’s stroke, developed an idea for cameras that detect warning signs of a recurring stroke. She won the $30,000 grand prize in the campus Big Ideas Contest and joined Berkeley SkyDeck, the university’s startup accelerator, whose main program invests $210,000 in each startup.
The university has also launched the UC Berkeley Chancellor’s Fund, a donor-funded venture fund owned by the university that invests in campus startups.
